stereotype

/STER-uh-type/ — stress on first syllable, rhymes with type · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified idea about what everyone in a certain group is like. It ignores the fact that the people in that group can actually be very different from one another.

The film pokes fun at the stereotype of the absent-minded scientist.

Example

When people assume that all teenagers are lazy and irresponsible without knowing them, they're applying a stereotype—ignoring how different teens actually are from one another.

Stereotype is more precise than 'assumption' or 'generalization' because it emphasizes that the idea is not just a personal guess but a fixed, widespread, oversimplified cultural belief. A generalization might be partly accurate; a stereotype distorts reality by treating an entire diverse group as if everyone in it is the same.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

prejudice: A prejudice is an unfair opinion formed before you have the facts, and it often carries hostile feeling toward its target. A stereotype is the fixed, oversimplified picture of a group — 'they are all alike' — that a prejudice often leans on for support.

cliché: A cliché is an expression or idea so overused it has gone stale — 'time heals all wounds.' Clichés are about tired words and plots. A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified belief about the people in a group, and it does real unfairness, not just boredom.

assumption: An assumption is something one person takes to be true without checking — a private guess about a situation or a single person. A stereotype is bigger and more public: a fixed, oversimplified picture of an entire group that many people share and repeat.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

individuality: the distinct qualities of one person

nuance: a subtle difference or fine distinction

Where it sits · how rigidly it labels a whole group

trait → pattern → generalization → stereotype

trait vs. stereotype: A trait is one quality a person truly has, while a stereotype forces a whole set of qualities onto an entire group.

pattern vs. stereotype: Noticing a pattern means observing what often happens, but a stereotype hardens that pattern into a fixed idea about everyone in a group.

generalization vs. stereotype: A generalization is a broad statement that may be partly true, while a stereotype is more rigid and unfair to individuals.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — stereo: solid, firm (Greek)

Root — type: impression, mold (Greek)

Put it together: Stereo- means 'solid' and type means 'impression or mold.' A stereotype was originally a solid metal printing plate that stamped the identical image over and over — just as a stereotype stamps one fixed image onto every member of a group.

Use the root in a new word: prototype: Engineers tested the delivery-drone prototype in a wind tunnel through the spring — proto- plus type, the same Greek mold root pressed into stereotype.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Stereotype is the right word when discussing fixed, oversimplified, widespread beliefs about entire groups—especially in discussions of bias and fairness. For a personal assumption about one person, use assumption. For a broad statement that might be accurate, generalization works. For harmful prejudicial thinking, prejudice is stronger, emphasizing intent to harm.
